items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S7910

SPONSOR: FUNKE
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the arts and cultural affairs law, in relation to music
licensing agreements

 
PURPOSE:

Relates to music licensing agreements

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1: Establishes a new title H in the arts and cultural affairs
law to regulate music licensing agreement, it contains definitions,
requires registration of agreements and members, regulates represen-
tative conduct and contracts, provides enforcement and statutory
construction.

Section 2: Establishes the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

In May of 2017, I conducted a Round Table discussion surrounding the
issues our wine and grape growers face in New York State. One of the
topics brought up by numerous winery owners had to do with Performing
Rights Societies those that represent copyright owners in the music
industry - and the fact that this industry is largely unregulated in New
York State and therefore the problems the wineries faced could not be
resolved without legislation. Following up that Round Table, I continued
to discuss the issue with those in the farm industry at all levels,
including statewide and those working on the issue at a national level.
These discussions led me to look at a new law Washington State imple-
mented in 2017 that establishes requirements for music licensing organ-
izations conducting business in their state.  This bill is based on that
law along with a few minor improvements based on their experience in
implementing.

Across New York state there are numerous businesses who use music in a
variety of ways. These businesses may include: bars, restaurants, winer-
ies, distilleries, breweries, retail establishments, fitness facilities
and countless others. The music they play could come from a live band or
a solo singer, recorded music might come from an iPod, Pandora, CDs, a
DJ or karaoke machine, among other options. In order for businesses to
use copyrighted music, they must obtain permission before playing a
songwriters music publicly according to United States Copyright Law. A
Performing Rights Society represent songwriters, composers and other
music publishers, and they issue the license to businesses wanting to
play the copyrighted music of their members.

The issue New York State businesses have had is in determining which
Performing Rights Society represents which songwriters, etc. Many times
they are issued a letter from one of these organizations demanding a sum
of money, or potentially a letter declaring that their business is being
sued. The goal of this legislation is not to prevent a Performing Rights
Society from being able to charge their fee, but it is to regulate their
practice and ensure businesses are provided with the information neces-
sary to enter into a binding contract.
 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New Bill

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect January 1, 2019.
